'''Colin Michael Foale''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|CBE}} ({{IPAc-en|f|oʊ|l}}; born 6 January 1957) is a British-American [[astrophysicist]] and a former [[NASA astronaut]].<ref name="nasa-bio">{{Cite web |date=August 2013 |title=C. Michael Foale |url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/foale_michael.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210507080036/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/foale_michael.pdf |archive-date=7 May 2021 |access-date=7 May 2021 |website=Biographical Data |publisher=[[Johnson Space Center]] / [[NASA]] |location=[[Houston, Texas]] }}</ref> He is a veteran of six space missions, and he is the only NASA astronaut to have flown extended missions aboard both [[Mir]] and the [[International Space Station]]. He was the second [[British people|Briton]] in space and the first to perform a space walk. Until 17 April 2008, he held the record for most time spent in space by a US citizen: 374 days, 11 hours, 19 minutes, and {{As of|2024|lc=y}} he held the cumulative-time-in-space record for a British citizen.{{citation needed|date=April 2016}}<!-- Leed and infobox are supposed to sum up article body, but time in space appears nowhere in body. -->

==Life and career==
Foale was born in [[Louth, Lincolnshire]], to a British father, Colin, and an American mother, Mary. His father was an [[RAF]] officer who retired with the rank of [[Air Commodore]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Parents cheer son's space stay |url=https://newsimg.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/cambridgeshire/3207896.stm |website=BBC News |access-date=20 November 2024 |date=20 October 2003}}</ref> Foale was raised in [[Cambridge]] and educated at [[The King's School, Canterbury]]. A member of the [[Air Training Corps]], he studied at [[Queens' College, Cambridge]] receiving a [[British undergraduate degree classification|first-class honours]] [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] degree in natural sciences in 1978  (later promoted to a [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge and Dublin)|Cambridge MA]]), and subsequently a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in laboratory astrophysics in 1982, where his supervisor was [[Alan Cook (physicist)|Alan Cook]].<ref name="foale-thesis">{{Cite thesis |last=Foale |first=Colin Michael |author-link=Michael Foale |date=23 February 1982 |title=The far-ultraviolet spectroscopy of molecules of astrophysical interest |url=https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/bitstreams/79481e0a-2310-4891-b1c1-d499ce66054b/download |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231130072815/https://api.repository.cam.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/79481e0a-2310-4891-b1c1-d499ce66054b/content |archive-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[University of Cambridge]] |doi=10.17863/CAM.695 |type=PhD }}</ref> When he left university, he "owned two pairs of jeans, a donkey jacket, a bicycle and a pilot's licence; which shows I had my priorities absolutely right".{{cn|date=January 2023}}

While a postgraduate student at Cambridge University, he participated in the organisation and execution of scientific scuba diving projects. Pursuing a career in the US Space Program, he moved to Houston, Texas to work on Space Shuttle navigation problems for [[McDonnell Douglas]]. In June 1983, Foale joined the NASA Johnson Space Center in the payload operations area of the Mission Operations Directorate. In his capacity as payload officer in the Mission Control Center, he was responsible for payload operations on Space Shuttle missions STS-51G, 51-I, 61-B and 61-C.

Born in the United Kingdom, Foale applied and was turned down twice as an astronaut candidate. After the [[Space Shuttle Challenger disaster|Space Shuttle ''Challenger'' disaster]] in January 1986, Foale changed his application [[essay]] from writing about his dreams to focusing on the realities of leadership faced by NASA, and was selected in 1987.{{cn|date=January 2023}}
[[Image:Foale ZeroG.jpg|left|thumb|Michael Foale (foreground) exercising on the [[International Space Station|ISS]]]]
 	
He flew on Space Shuttle missions [[STS-45]] (1992),<ref name="sts-45">{{Cite web |date=1 September 2023 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Sandra L. |title=STS-45 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-45/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231127185210/https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-45/ |archive-date=27 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> [[STS-56]] (1993)<ref name="sts-56">{{Cite web |date=20 September 2023 |editor-last=Mitchell |editor-first=Narumi J. |title=STS-56 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-56/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231127185314/https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-56/ |archive-date=27 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> and [[STS-63]] (1995).<ref name="sts-63">{{Cite web |date=22 August 2023 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Sandra L. |title=STS-63 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-63/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231127185338/https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-63/ |archive-date=27 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> In the last mission, he undertook a four-hour [[Extra-vehicular activity|EVA]]. He was then selected for an extended mission aboard the Russian [[Mir]] space station.

Launched by [[STS-84]]<ref name="sts-84">{{Cite web |date=22 August 2023 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Sandra L. |title=STS-84 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-84/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231127185456/https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-84/ |archive-date=27 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> and returned by [[STS-86]],<ref name="sts-86">{{Cite web |date=22 August 2023 |editor-last=Johnson |editor-first=Sandra L. |title=STS-86 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-86/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231127185501/https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-86/ |archive-date=27 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> Foale spent four months on Mir in 1997 during the Mir 23 and Mir 24 missions. During Mir 23, the station's [[Spektr]] module was struck by a [[Progress spacecraft|Progress]] resupply vessel.<ref name="bbc-20160622">{{Cite news |last=Foale |first=Michael |author-link=Michael Foale |date=22 June 2016 |title=Mir Spacecraft: Worst collision in the history of space flight |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/av/magazine-36549109 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230514070744/https://www.bbc.com/news/av/magazine-36549109 |archive-date=14 May 2023 }}</ref> Using knowledge from his physics degree, Foale made calculations of how the stars were moving past his fixed-point [[thumb]] reference on a window, and was thus able to advise Russian ground control of how to stop the resulting roll.{{cn|date=January 2023}} The two Russian cosmonauts of Mir 23, [[Vasily Tsibliyev]] and [[Aleksandr Lazutkin]] were planned to conduct an intravehicular activity (IVA) to inspect the collision damage from the interior of the space station, but this IVA was actually carried out by Mir EO-24 crew. After the [[Mir EO-24]] crew exchange, Soyuz TM-26 with all three crew aboard was undocked, repositioned and re-docked. Foale acted as photographer during the operation. Foale and Russian cosmonaut [[Anatoly Solovyev]] also conducted a six-hour EVA in Russian [[Orlan_space_suit|Orlan spacesuits]] to inspect exterior damage to the Spektr module. Station damage produced significant risk to EVA suit integrity. For his efforts, he was awarded the [[Yuri A. Gagarin Gold Medal]] by the [[Fédération Aéronautique Internationale]].<ref name="fai-awards">{{Cite web |title=FAI Awards received by C. Michael FOALE (USA) |url=http://www.fai.org/awards/recipient.asp?id=26310 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110518094204/http://www.fai.org/awards/recipient.asp?id=26310 |archive-date=18 May 2011 |publisher=[[Fédération Aéronautique Internationale]] }}</ref> Subsequently, Mir's primary and backup oxygen generation systems failed, but these were successfully repaired by the crew. The station also experienced computer failures and problems orientating the solar arrays at the correct angle to the Sun. All these difficulties combined to produce what, looking back 20 years later, was arguably, the most dangerous long-duration mission for a NASA astronaut. The problems encountered by Foale and his predecessor aboard Mir, [[Jerry Linenger]], resulted in intense political pressure on NASA. The final decision between the termination of NASA crewing of Mir with Foale's departure, or his scheduled replacement by [[David Wolf (astronaut)|David Wolf]] was only made by NASA Administrator [[Daniel Goldin]] the night before the launch of [[STS-86]].

In 1999, Foale was a member of Space Shuttle mission [[STS-103]],<ref name="sts-103">{{Cite web |date=26 September 2023 |editor-last=Belleville |editor-first=Michelle |title=STS-103 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-103/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231127185554/https://www.nasa.gov/mission/sts-103/ |archive-date=27 November 2023 |access-date=30 November 2023 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> during which he conducted an eight-hour [[spacewalk]] to replace components of the [[Hubble Space Telescope]]. In 2003, Foale was named commander of [[International Space Station]] [[Expedition 8]] with cosmonaut [[Aleksandr Kaleri]]. During their six-month tour of duty on the station, Foale and Kaleri carried out a 4-hour Russian EVA in Orlan-M space suits to install experiments outside the Service Module. The EVA was cut short when significant amounts of water in Kaleri's helmet prevented further work.  Expedition 8 ended on 29 April 2004. For about a year, Foale was Deputy Associate Administrator for Exploration Operations at NASA HQ, [[Washington D.C.]] He then supported Soyuz and ISS operations and [[spacesuit]] development for NASA in Houston.

In August 2013, it was announced that Foale was leaving the agency after a 26-year career to work on developing an [[electric aircraft]] to advance [[Green technology|green aviation technology]].<ref name="bbc-20130810">{{Cite news |last=Amos |first=Jonathan |date=10 August 2013 |title=Astronaut Michael Foale retires from Nasa |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-23645168 |url-status=live |access-date=10 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230812192107/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-23645168 |archive-date=12 August 2023 }}</ref> Since leaving NASA, Foale has become actively involved in the running of the International Space Schools Education Trust, especially their Mission Discovery and trips to [[Star City, Russia]], giving unique experiences to students around the world. Mission Discovery is held each year at the Guy's Campus at King's College London.

==Honours==
Foale was awarded an [[honorary degree]] by the [[University of Lincolnshire and Humberside]] in July 2000<ref>{{cite web |url=http://homepages.enterprise.net/rogerp/famous.html |website=Roger P@rsons' "Lincolnshire World" |title=p@rsons_world of Famous Lincolnshire people... |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071015195746/http://homepages.enterprise.net/rogerp/famous.html |archivedate=15 October 2007 |accessdate=15 January 2016}}{{rs|date=January 2023}}</ref> and an honorary [[Doctor of Science]] degree by the [[University of Kent]] in September 2000.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.kent.ac.uk/congregations/honorary-graduates/archive |title=Archive of honorary graduates |publisher=University of Kent |accessdate=17 January 2023}}</ref> He was invested as a Commander of the [[Order of the British Empire]] in the diplomatic list of the [[New Year Honours]] in December 2004.<ref name="bbc-20041231">{{Cite news |date=31 December 2004 |title=British-born astronaut given CBE |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/4135695.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230301033938/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/4135695.stm |archive-date=1 March 2023 }}</ref>

It is possible he has been patron to a pastoral house at the Folkestone Academy in Kent, which is also named after him.{{citation needed|date=January 2016}} A street in Foale's birth town was named Michael Foale Lane.<ref name="louthleader-20130812">{{cite news |last1=Kinnaird |first1=Sam |title=Louth-born NASA astronaut Michael Foale retires |url=https://www.louthleader.co.uk/news/louth-born-nasa-astronaut-michael-foale-retires-1-5377624 |url-status=dead |access-date=14 January 2019 |work=Louth Leader |date=12 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180615083525/https://www.louthleader.co.uk/news/louth-born-nasa-astronaut-michael-foale-retires-1-5377624 |archive-date=15 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="lincolnshirelive-20170612">{{cite news |last1=O'Flinn |first1=Holly |title=Louth astronaut added to NASA's Hall of Fame |url=https://www.lincolnshirelive.co.uk/news/local-news/louth-astronaut-added-nasas-hall-105811 |url-status=live |access-date=14 January 2019 |work=Lincolnshire Live |date=12 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220625152108/https://www.lincolnshirelive.co.uk/news/local-news/louth-astronaut-added-nasas-hall-105811 |archive-date=25 June 2022 }}</ref><ref name="grimsbylive-20170609">{{cite news |last1=Craig |first1=Peter |title=Louth astronaut mocked by Stephen Fry for space ambition is inducted into NASA hall of fame |url=https://www.grimsbytelegraph.co.uk/news/grimsby-news/rocketman-beams-nasa-hall-fame-103868 |url-status=live |access-date=14 January 2019 |work=Grimsby Live |date=9 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220310072137/https://www.grimsbytelegraph.co.uk/news/grimsby-news/rocketman-beams-nasa-hall-fame-103868 |archive-date=10 March 2022}}</ref>

Foale and [[Ellen Ochoa]] were announced as the 2017 class of the [[United States Astronaut Hall of Fame]].<ref name="floridatoday-20170519">{{Cite news |last=Dean |first=James |date=19 May 2017 |title=NASA's Foale, Ochoa welcomed into Astronaut Hall of Fame |work=[[Florida Today]] |url=https://www.floridatoday.com/story/tech/science/space/2017/05/19/nasas-foale-ochoa-welcomed-astronaut-hall-fame/101903844/ |url-status=live |access-date=30 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231130081733/https://www.floridatoday.com/story/tech/science/space/2017/05/19/nasas-foale-ochoa-welcomed-astronaut-hall-fame/101903844/ |archive-date=30 November 2023 }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Married with two children, Foale and his family live in [[Seabrook, Texas]]. He is fluent in [[Russian language|Russian]]. Foale is qualified to fly fixed-wing aeroplanes, gliders, and helicopters. He has never owned a brand-new car, though he has always wanted one, and his hobbies include [[windsurfing]], [[gliding]], and [[cross-country skiing]].

Foale was the driver of a car in 1980 in [[Yugoslavia]], when a truck accidentally veered across the road and smashed into his car, killing his girlfriend and his brother.{{cn|date=January 2023}}
His father, Colin Foale, wrote a book in 1999 titled ''Waystation to the Stars'' about the astronaut's experiences on Mir.

In his spare time, he has also worked with the International Space School Educational Trust (ISSET). This involvement is through him taking up the role of the resident astronaut during many of the [[Mission Discovery]] programmes operated by ISSET, when Foale shares his experiences of being in space with teenagers, while at the same time helping them to learn new skills. He does this throughout the period of the time the programme runs.<ref name="ayrshire-foundation">{{cite web |title=Ayrshire to Host Out of This World Opportunity |publisher=[[Ayrshire College]] |url=http://www1.ayrshire.ac.uk/news/news-events/2016/ayrshire-to-host-out-of-this-world-opportunity/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201143528/http://www1.ayrshire.ac.uk/news/news-events/2016/ayrshire-to-host-out-of-this-world-opportunity/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=1 December 2016 |access-date=17 January 2023 }}</ref>
